provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate stood at 7.0% in the June Labour Force Survey while wage growth decelerated to +2.1% in May, down 2.1 percentage points from +4.2% — the wage slowdown1 sits across employment-sensitive sectors that the project database tracks in volume, including 115 healthcare and 222 infrastructure files2. The 2026 Ontario Budget forecasts 2026 real GDP growth near 1.0% and the unemployment rate easing from 7.7% in 2025 toward 7.4% in 2026.

Housing starts fell 8.4% to 62,735 units SAAR as of June 15, the steepest decline among the large provinces this period — the residential contraction3 runs alongside a budget that adds $111.3B in total infrastructure spending over 2025-26 to 2027-28, up $13.6B from the 2025 FES and including an additional $11.0B in planned transit4. The database tracks 694 Ontario projects, of which 91 qualify above the $500M threshold and total roughly $297.2B; infrastructure (222 files) and transport_logistics (134) are the two largest categories by count.

Ontario CPI registered +2.9% year-over-year on the May reference period — the print5 accompanies a capital pipeline led by the Adaptive Phased Management Deep Geological Repository, the province's largest tracked file at $26.0B in Proposed status2. Agnico Eagle's $14B Ontario mining capital program is Proposed in the Timmins region, while Honda's $15B EV and battery complex is marked Cancelled in the database after an indefinite 2026 suspension.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Infrastructure and transport lead Ontario's tracked pipeline by count — the database records 222 infrastructure and 134 transport_logistics projects, with the Ontario Line and GO Expansion both Under Construction in the Toronto area2. Healthcare (115 files) and the 41 mining files sit in employment-sensitive and commodity-exposed categories; Agnico Eagle's $14B capital program (Proposed) anchors the mining count, while the Cancelled $15B Honda EV complex underscores manufacturing's CAD/USD and auto-sector exposure.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Ontario's labour market carried a 7.0% unemployment rate, a 64.7% participation rate, and a 60.2% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth slowed to +2.1% in May, a 2.1-percentage-point deceleration from +4.2%1. The 2026 Budget notes 2025 added roughly +80,900 net jobs, nearly all private sector, and forecasts a softer 2026 labour market on slower population growth, with employment growth near 0.5%4.
provinces.consumerPulse: Ontario CPI ran at +2.9% year-over-year on the May reference period, the highest among the large provinces this period — the inflation read5 accompanies decelerating wage growth of +2.1%, narrowing the gap between price and pay changes for Ontario households. Housing starts at 62,735 SAAR (-8.4%) point to a residential market cooling against a budget-backed infrastructure and transit build-out.
provinces.marketContext: Ontario's pipeline spans 694 tracked projects, with 91 qualifying above the $500M threshold totalling ~$297.2B; infrastructure (222), transport_logistics (134) and healthcare (115) lead by count. Rate-sensitive transit and infrastructure plans dominate, while mining and manufacturing files carry commodity and CAD/USD exposure.
provinces.tradeExposure: Ontario's economy is anchored in auto manufacturing and advanced manufacturing with heavy U.S. export exposure; the Cancelled $15B Honda EV and battery complex and the 41 tracked mining files tie capital decisions to CAD/USD and metals prices.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec's unemployment rate held at 5.6% in the June Labour Force Survey while CPI ran at +1.5% year-over-year, the second-lowest provincial inflation rate this period — wage growth1 decelerated to +4.7% in May, down 1.2 percentage points from +5.9%. The province's quarterly provincial accounts (qc_real_gdp at $486,872.7M, qc_nominal_gdp at $652,636M) carry a 2025-10-01 reference period and are cited as such rather than as current-week figures.

Hydro-Quebec reported Q1 2026 net income of $1,850M, down $206M year-over-year, alongside a record quarterly investment of $1.6B — the utility2 launched a financing program exceeding $5B with the Canada Infrastructure Bank and National Bank for Indigenous wind participation and announced five wind partnerships totalling more than 10,000 MW. Its Action Plan 2035 targets $135-160B in investment, and the database tracks 49 Quebec power_energy projects within 95 qualifying files above the $250M threshold totalling roughly $120.3B3.

Quebec's tracked pipeline spans 502 projects, the largest categories by count being education (110), infrastructure (99) and power_energy (49) — Parc eolien zone Chamouchouane ($9.0B, Proposed) ranks among the largest tracked wind files3, while the Canada-Quebec federal infrastructure funding transfer ($10B, Proposed) and the Montreal Metro Blue Line Extension ($4.9B, Under Construction, 2031 target) anchor the rate-sensitive transit pipeline4.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and education lead Quebec's tracked count, with Hydro-Quebec anchoring energy-sector exposure — the database records 49 power_energy and 110 education files3. Hydro-Quebec's record $1.6B quarterly investment, Action Plan 2035 ($135-160B target), and five wind partnerships exceeding 10,000 MW concentrate capital in renewables; copper and electrical-equipment input costs flow through to the wind and grid capital plans2.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Quebec recorded a 5.6% unemployment rate, a 64.1% participation rate, and a 60.6% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth eased to +4.7% in May, a 1.2-percentage-point deceleration from +5.9%1. The 5.6% unemployment rate is among the lowest of the large provinces, sitting below Ontario's 7.0% and British Columbia's 6.8% this period.
provinces.consumerPulse: Quebec CPI registered +1.5% year-over-year, the second-lowest provincial inflation rate this period — the inflation read1 accompanies wage growth of +4.7%, leaving pay changes running ahead of price changes for Quebec households. Building permits totalled $2.90B in April, up from $2.60B the prior period.
provinces.marketContext: Quebec's pipeline spans 502 tracked projects, with 95 qualifying above the $250M threshold totalling ~$120.3B; education (110), infrastructure (99) and power_energy (49) lead by count. Hydro-Quebec's Action Plan 2035 and five wind partnerships anchor power-sector exposure, while the $10B Canada-Quebec transfer drives rate-sensitive transit.
provinces.tradeExposure: Quebec exports hydroelectric power, aluminum, and aerospace products with significant U.S. market exposure; Hydro-Quebec's grid expansion and the wind partnerships tie capital plans to copper and electrical-equipment input costs.

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.analysis:
Alberta posted the highest provincial participation rate at 69.1% and a lowest-tier CPI of +1.1% in the latest prints, with unemployment at 6.6% — wage growth1 decelerated to +4.8% in May, down 1.7 percentage points from +6.5%. GDP growth of +2.7% sits alongside 700 tracked Alberta projects, of which 176 qualify above the $200M threshold and total roughly $416.8B2.

Canada and Alberta signed an MOU announced 2026-05-15 covering a proposed bitumen-to-Asia pipeline, the Pathways Alliance carbon capture project, and a nuclear strategy, a package described as more than $126B in investment — the MOU3 sets a 2026-07-01 deadline for Alberta to submit a proposal for a pipeline of at least 1M bbl/day to the federal Major Projects Office, and resets the Pathways CCUS target to 16 megatonnes per year, a 77% reduction from the 68 Mt/yr figure announced in 2021. The Pathways Alliance CCS Hub Phase 1 ($16.5B, Proposed) ranks among the largest tracked power_energy files2.

Two C$50.0B proposed files anchor the top of Alberta's tracked pipeline — the Peace River Nuclear Power Project and the Olds AI Data Centre Hub (capped) — power_energy (161 files), government (141) and infrastructure (104) lead by count2, and WTI and WCS price movements flow through to oil-sands and CCUS capital plans. Housing starts fell 4.9% to 46,064 units SAAR as of June 15.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy lead Alberta's tracked count at 161 files, with the Pathways CCUS hub and two C$50.0B nuclear and data-centre files at the top of the pipeline — the database records 161 power_energy, 141 government and 104 infrastructure projects2. The proposed bitumen-to-Asia pipeline (at least 1M bbl/day) carries oil-price and export-differential exposure, while the $19.0B Telus province-wide telecom program and $12.0B Wonder Valley AI data centre park add capital-cost and power-demand sensitivity3.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Alberta carried the highest provincial participation rate at 69.1%, a 64.6% employment rate, and a 6.6% unemployment rate in the June LFS — wage growth eased to +4.8% in May, a 1.7-percentage-point deceleration from +6.5%1. The 69.1% participation rate leads all provinces, reflecting the province's energy and construction labour base.
provinces.consumerPulse: Alberta CPI ran at +1.1% year-over-year, in the lowest tier of provincial inflation this period — the inflation read1 accompanies wage growth of +4.8%, leaving pay changes well ahead of price changes for Alberta households. Building permits totalled $1.63B in April, up from $1.58B the prior period.
provinces.marketContext: Alberta's pipeline spans 700 tracked projects, with 176 qualifying above the $200M threshold totalling ~$416.8B; power_energy (161), government (141) and infrastructure (104) lead by count. WTI and WCS movements flow through to oil-sands and the Pathways Alliance CCS Hub, while the proposed bitumen-to-Asia pipeline carries oil-price and export-differential exposure.
provinces.tradeExposure: Alberta exports crude oil, bitumen, and natural gas with heavy U.S. and emerging Asian-market exposure; the proposed >=1M bbl/day bitumen-to-Asia pipeline and Pathways CCUS hub tie capital decisions to WTI, WCS, and export differentials.

provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.analysis:
British Columbia's wage growth of +1.5% in May, down 1.0 percentage point from +2.5%, was the lowest provincial wage growth this period — the deceleration1 accompanies an unemployment rate of 6.8% and the largest qualifying project pipeline of any province. The database tracks 648 B.C. projects, of which 311 qualify above the $175M threshold and total roughly $508.1B2.

Canada, B.C., and LNG Canada reached an enhanced investment co-operation agreement to progress toward a potential 2026 Final Investment Decision on LNG Canada's Phase 2 expansion — the agreement3 sits alongside 122 power_energy and 101 mining files leading the tracked pipeline by count2. B.C. approved new mine permits cited at more than $3B in private investment across the Mount Milligan and Copper Mountain extensions and Eskay Creek; Kitimat Clean Oil Refinery ($22.0B, Under Review) and Site C Hydro ($16.0B, Under Construction) are among the largest tracked power_energy files.

Housing starts stood at 40,133 units SAAR, down 2.4%, as reported home sales fell more than 10% in Q1 2026 and rental asking prices declined for a 29th consecutive month — the residential data4 runs against CPI of +2.7% year-over-year and a 'Look West' major-projects acceleration strategy advancing through the spring legislative session5.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and mining lead British Columbia's tracked count, with LNG and hydro anchoring energy-sector exposure — the database records 122 power_energy, 101 mining and 71 residential files2. Natural-gas prices and LNG export economics flow through to LNG Canada Phase 2 and the $22.0B Kitimat Clean refinery, while copper and gold prices drive the more than $3B in newly permitted mine investment at Mount Milligan, Copper Mountain, and Eskay Creek3.
provinces.labourDeepDive: British Columbia recorded a 6.8% unemployment rate, a 64.9% participation rate, and a 60.5% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth of +1.5% in May, down 1.0 percentage point from +2.5%, was the lowest provincial wage growth this period1. The wage deceleration accompanies a residential market where home sales fell more than 10% in Q1 2026.
provinces.consumerPulse: British Columbia CPI ran at +2.7% year-over-year while wage growth slowed to +1.5%, the lowest provincial wage growth this period — the gap1 leaves price changes running ahead of pay changes for B.C. households. Rental asking prices declined for a 29th consecutive month and reported home sales fell more than 10% in Q1 20264.
provinces.marketContext: British Columbia's pipeline spans 648 tracked projects, with 311 qualifying above the $175M threshold totalling ~$508.1B, the largest qualifying pipeline of any province; power_energy (122), mining (101) and residential (71) lead by count. Natural-gas prices and LNG export economics flow through to LNG Canada Phase 2 and the $22.0B Kitimat Clean refinery.
provinces.tradeExposure: British Columbia exports liquefied natural gas, metallurgical coal, lumber, and metals with Asian-market and U.S. exposure; LNG Canada Phase 2 economics tie to natural-gas prices, while the >$3B in new mine permits ties to copper and gold prices.

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan posted the second-highest provincial GDP growth at +3.4% and a lowest-tier CPI of +1.1%, while housing starts fell 17.6% to 4,472 units SAAR, the sharpest provincial decline this period — the housing drop1 contrasts with a qualifying pipeline concentrated in potash mining rather than residential construction. The database tracks 154 Saskatchewan projects, of which 48 qualify above the $45M threshold and total roughly $52.9B2.

BHP booked a $2.3B impairment on the Jansen potash mine, citing cost and timing overruns on the Stage 2 expansion — the impairment3 leaves Jansen Stage 1 on track for first production mid-2027 at projected combined output of 8.5 Mtpa, roughly 10% of global potash, at the lowest unit cost among Canadian potash mines (US$114-130/t). Jansen Potash Project (C$13.9B, Under Construction) is the province's largest tracked file, and CN announced rail service on 2026-06-05 to connect Jansen production to global markets4.

Infrastructure, power, and mining lead Saskatchewan's tracked count at 41, 28, and 27 files respectively — potash prices drive the Jansen capital program (C$13.9B Under Construction, plus the $6.9B Stage 2 expansion that just absorbed a $2.3B impairment)2, while the proposed C$8.6B Thor alumina facility adds aluminum and commodity-price exposure. Wage growth eased to +4.1% in May, down 0.4 percentage points.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Mining anchors Saskatchewan's value exposure through the Jansen potash program despite broad-based GDP strength — the database records 41 infrastructure, 28 power_energy and 27 mining files2. Potash prices drive Jansen (C$13.9B Under Construction plus the $6.9B Stage 2 expansion), while the proposed C$8.6B Thor alumina facility and the $2.0B FCL renewable diesel plant add aluminum and energy exposure3.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Saskatchewan carried a 6.2% unemployment rate, a 66.8% participation rate, and a 62.6% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth eased to +4.1% in May, down 0.4 percentage points from +4.5%1. The labour data accompanies GDP growth of +3.4%, the second-highest among provinces, even as housing starts fell 17.6%.
provinces.consumerPulse: Saskatchewan CPI ran at +1.1% year-over-year, in the lowest tier of provincial inflation this period — the inflation read1 accompanies wage growth of +4.1%, leaving pay changes ahead of price changes for Saskatchewan households. Building permits totalled $254M in April, down from $320M the prior period, alongside the 17.6% housing-starts decline.
provinces.marketContext: Saskatchewan's pipeline spans 154 tracked projects, with 48 qualifying above the $45M threshold totalling ~$52.9B; infrastructure (41), power_energy (28) and mining (27) lead by count. Potash prices drive the Jansen capital program, and the proposed C$8.6B Thor alumina facility adds aluminum and commodity-price exposure.
provinces.tradeExposure: Saskatchewan exports potash, uranium, oil, and agricultural commodities with global market reach; the Jansen potash program ties capital plans to potash prices, with CN rail service connecting production to export markets.

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.analysis:
Manitoba posted the lowest provincial unemployment rate at 5.5% in the June Labour Force Survey, while CPI tied highest with Prince Edward Island at +3.5% year-over-year — the low jobless rate1 accompanies the largest tracked record count of any province at 1,962 projects, reflecting EA-registry granularity. Of those, 88 qualify above the $40M threshold and total roughly $44.0B2.

Manitoba Budget 2026, tabled 2026-03-24, includes $1.17B in Manitoba Hydro capital investment, a new $10M Churchill Catalyst Fund, and $1.4M for the Manitoba Mineral Development Fund — the budget3 adds federal-provincial funding toward a critical-minerals storage facility at the Port of Churchill, and the province committed a further $2.5M to advance new mining and critical-mineral opportunities. The database tracks 278 Manitoba power_energy projects within the qualifying set2.

Infrastructure, agriculture, and power lead Manitoba's tracked count at 617, 306, and 278 files respectively — the Manitoba Large-Scale Hydroelectric Dam ($18.0B, Proposed) is the largest tracked file2, while the C$4.0B anhydrous ammonia facility and C$2.2B Morris natural-gas pipeline add natural-gas and fertilizer-price sensitivity. Housing starts fell 5.9% to 7,361 units SAAR and wage growth eased to +1.8% in May.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and infrastructure lead Manitoba's tracked count, anchored by Manitoba Hydro and the proposed large-scale hydro dam — the database records 617 infrastructure, 306 agriculture and 278 power_energy files2. Manitoba Hydro capital ($1.17B in the 2026 budget) and the proposed $18.0B large-scale hydro dam anchor power-sector exposure, while the $4.0B anhydrous ammonia facility and $2.2B Morris natural-gas pipeline add fertilizer and natural-gas-price sensitivity3.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Manitoba recorded the lowest provincial unemployment rate at 5.5%, a 66.8% participation rate, and a 63.1% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth eased to +1.8% in May, down 0.6 percentage points from +2.4%1. The 5.5% jobless rate is the lowest of any province this period, below Quebec's 5.6%.
provinces.consumerPulse: Manitoba CPI ran at +3.5% year-over-year, tied with Prince Edward Island for the highest provincial inflation this period — the inflation read1 sits above wage growth of +1.8%, leaving price changes running ahead of pay changes for Manitoba households. Building permits totalled $387M in April, down from $461M the prior period.
provinces.marketContext: Manitoba's tracked roster is the largest in the country at 1,962 projects (reflecting EA-registry granularity), with 88 qualifying above the $40M threshold totalling ~$44.0B; infrastructure (617), agriculture (306) and power_energy (278) lead by count. Manitoba Hydro capital and the proposed $18.0B large-scale hydro dam anchor power-sector exposure.
provinces.tradeExposure: Manitoba exports agricultural commodities, hydroelectric power, and processed foods with U.S. and inter-provincial reach; the critical-minerals storage facility at the Port of Churchill positions the province for northern mineral export logistics.

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.analysis:
Nova Scotia recorded GDP growth of +2.7% and is one of only two provinces with rising wage growth this period, at +4.2% in May, up 0.3 percentage points — the wage acceleration1 accompanies an unemployment rate of 7.1% and a pipeline anchored by power and defence. The database tracks 339 Nova Scotia projects, of which 58 qualify above the $25M threshold and total roughly $22.7B2.

Nova Scotia's offshore-wind framework advanced, with the province planning to offer licences for up to 5 GW from its first call for bids in 2026 and subsequent calls for up to an additional 10 GW — a Nova Scotia-Massachusetts agreement signed 2026-02-04 targets supplying the state with offshore-wind power3, and the database tracks 113 Nova Scotia power_energy projects. Bear Head Energy ($8.0B, Proposed) is the largest tracked file2.

Defence and shipbuilding anchor the province's pipeline alongside the offshore-wind build-out — the Canadian Submarine Program (Hanwha Ocean proposal, $6.3B, Proposed) and Canadian Naval Radar Procurement ($2.5B, Proposed) are tracked alongside the roughly $70B, 30-year Irving Shipbuilding combat-vessel program4. Housing starts stood at 7,241 units SAAR, down 2.5%, against CPI of +1.8% year-over-year.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and defence lead Nova Scotia's value exposure through offshore wind and shipbuilding — the database records 113 power_energy, 82 mining and 48 infrastructure files2. The offshore-wind framework (up to 5 GW first call, plus up to 10 GW in subsequent calls) and the $8.0B Bear Head Energy file anchor power-sector exposure, while defence procurement — the $6.3B submarine proposal, $2.5B naval radar, and the ~$70B Irving combat-vessel program — adds a large policy-driven shipbuilding pipeline4.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Nova Scotia carried a 7.1% unemployment rate, a 61.7% participation rate, and a 57.3% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth rose to +4.2% in May, up 0.3 percentage points from +3.9%, making the province one of two with accelerating wage growth this period1. The 7.1% unemployment rate sits among the higher provincial readings this period.
provinces.consumerPulse: Nova Scotia CPI ran at +1.8% year-over-year while wage growth rose to +4.2%, one of two provinces with accelerating pay this period — the gap1 leaves pay changes running ahead of price changes for Nova Scotia households. Building permits totalled $292M in April, up from $243M the prior period.
provinces.marketContext: Nova Scotia's pipeline spans 339 tracked projects, with 58 qualifying above the $25M threshold totalling ~$22.7B; power_energy (113), mining (82) and infrastructure (48) lead by count. The offshore-wind framework and the $8.0B Bear Head Energy file anchor power-sector exposure, while defence procurement adds a large policy-driven shipbuilding pipeline.
provinces.tradeExposure: Nova Scotia's emerging offshore-wind framework targets power supply to Massachusetts under a 2026-02-04 agreement, while seafood and forestry exports add U.S. exposure; defence procurement ties to federal shipbuilding programs.

provinces.name: New Brunswick
provinces.analysis:
New Brunswick posted the lowest CPI in Canada at +0.6% year-over-year and is one of two provinces with rising housing starts, up 0.3% to 5,860 units SAAR — the low inflation1 accompanies an unemployment rate of 7.2% and a smaller qualifying pipeline. The database tracks 176 New Brunswick projects, of which 58 qualify above the $20M threshold and total roughly $7.4B, the smallest qualifying provincial value east of the territories2.

New Brunswick's 2026-27 budget, 'Foundation for the Future', projects a $1.4B deficit equal to 2.7% of GDP, with $710M in new health-care spending and funding to prepare for additional nuclear development at Point Lepreau — the budget3 notes net debt-to-GDP is expected to breach 30% in FY2026/27 and rise toward 36% by FY2028/29. Defence and forestry lead the largest tracked files: Saint John Pulp Mill Upgrades ($1.1B, Under Review) and CFB Gagetown Recapitalization ($1.06B, Approved)4.

Infrastructure, tourism, and government lead New Brunswick's tracked count after a large 'Other' bucket of 53 files — forestry exposure runs through the $1.1B Saint John Pulp Mill upgrades (lumber and pulp prices), while defence procurement at CFB Gagetown adds a federal, policy-driven pipeline2. Wage growth edged up to +3.6% in May, up 0.1 percentage points.

provinces.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador posted the highest provincial unemployment rate at 9.6% and the lowest provincial wage growth at +0.9% in May, down 0.3 percentage points — the labour data1 accompanies the highest net-debt-to-GDP ratio of any province at roughly 44%. The database tracks 1,531 NL projects, of which 68 qualify above the $17M threshold and total roughly $88.5B2.

Newfoundland and Labrador reached agreements on life-of-field benefits, royalties, and an equity option with Equinor and BP to advance Bay du Nord, providing up to $6.4B in direct provincial revenue in the first phase — the agreement3 sets recoverable resources at roughly 430 million barrels, with sanction targeted 2027 and first oil around 2031. The province opened a call for bids on 16 offshore exploration parcels and allocated $90M over three years to an Offshore Exploration Fund4.

LNG and offshore oil dominate the province's value exposure, with Placentia Bay LNG (C$32.0B, Proposed) and Burin Peninsula EverWind Green Fuels (C$16.0B, Proposed) leading the tracked power_energy pipeline — infrastructure (258 files), transport_logistics (236) and mining (223) lead by count2, while the C$4.2B Long Harbour nickel plant adds base-metals exposure. Housing starts stood at 1,242 units SAAR, down 3.9%, against CPI of +2.9% year-over-year.
provinces.sectorHighlights: LNG and offshore oil dominate Newfoundland and Labrador's value exposure — the database records 258 infrastructure, 236 transport_logistics and 223 mining files by count2. Placentia Bay LNG (C$32.0B) and Grassy Point LNG ($10.0B) carry natural-gas-price sensitivity, while Bay du Nord ties provincial revenue to oil prices and the targeted 2027 sanction; the C$4.2B Long Harbour nickel plant adds base-metals exposure3.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Newfoundland and Labrador carried the highest provincial unemployment rate at 9.6%, a 56.7% participation rate, and a 51.3% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth of +0.9% in May, down 0.3 percentage points from +1.2%, was the lowest provincial wage growth this period1. The 9.6% jobless rate is the highest among the provinces, above New Brunswick's 7.2% and Nova Scotia's 7.1%.
provinces.consumerPulse: Newfoundland and Labrador CPI ran at +2.9% year-over-year while wage growth slowed to +0.9%, the lowest provincial wage growth this period — the gap1 leaves price changes running well ahead of pay changes for NL households. Building permits totalled $49M in April, up from $44M the prior period.
provinces.marketContext: Newfoundland and Labrador's tracked roster spans 1,531 projects, with 68 qualifying above the $17M threshold totalling ~$88.5B; infrastructure (258), transport_logistics (236) and mining (223) lead by count. LNG and offshore oil dominate value exposure, with Bay du Nord tying provincial revenue to oil prices.
provinces.tradeExposure: Newfoundland and Labrador exports offshore oil, iron ore, and seafood with global market reach; Bay du Nord and the offshore exploration bid call tie provincial revenue to oil prices, while LNG proposals carry natural-gas-price exposure.

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.analysis:
Prince Edward Island posted the highest provincial GDP growth at +3.6%, the largest housing-starts increase at +10.0% to 1,153 units SAAR, and the highest provincial wage level at +7.6% in May — the across-the-board strength1 accompanies CPI of +3.5% year-over-year, tied highest with Manitoba. The database tracks 86 PEI projects, of which 80 qualify above the $5M threshold and total roughly $1.9B, the smallest provincial qualifying value2.

PEI's 2026 budget, tabled 2026-04-14, adds a new personal income-tax bracket above $200k, higher property taxes and insurance premiums on non-resident owners projected at roughly $2M, and ends the energy-rebate program in June — the budget3 sits alongside a 10-year energy strategy (2026-2035) to expand on-Island renewables, where wind already supplies roughly 99% of current generation across about 268 MW installed4.

Infrastructure, tourism, and power lead PEI's tracked count at 40, 17, and 13 files respectively — wind dominates the energy mix, so PEI wind and transmission files (PEIEC Wind Farm #5, the Northumberland Strait submarine transmission system) carry power-price and capital-cost exposure rather than commodity exposure2. The $212.0M MDS Coating Technologies facility expansion (Approved) at Slemon Park is the province's largest tracked file.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Wind dominates Prince Edward Island's energy mix, shaping the province's power and transmission files — the database records 40 infrastructure, 17 tourism_culture and 13 power_energy files2. With wind at roughly 99% of generation across about 268 MW installed, PEI wind and transmission files (PEIEC Wind Farm #5, the Northumberland Strait submarine transmission system, the $180.0M Charlottetown district-energy facility) carry power-price and capital-cost exposure rather than commodity exposure4.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Prince Edward Island carried a 6.7% unemployment rate, a 66.5% participation rate, and a 62.0% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth of +7.6% in May, down 1.0 percentage point from +8.6%, was the highest provincial wage level this period1. The wage strength accompanies the highest provincial GDP growth at +3.6%.
provinces.consumerPulse: Prince Edward Island CPI ran at +3.5% year-over-year, tied with Manitoba for the highest provincial inflation, while wage growth led all provinces at +7.6% — the gap1 leaves pay changes running ahead of price changes for PEI households. Housing starts rose 10.0% to 1,153 units SAAR, the largest provincial increase this period.
provinces.marketContext: Prince Edward Island's pipeline spans 86 tracked projects, with 80 qualifying above the $5M threshold totalling ~$1.9B, the smallest provincial qualifying value; infrastructure (40), tourism_culture (17) and power_energy (13) lead by count. Wind dominates the energy mix at ~99% of generation, so PEI files carry power-price and capital-cost exposure rather than commodity exposure.
provinces.tradeExposure: Prince Edward Island's economy is primarily domestic-facing, anchored in agriculture (potatoes), seafood, and tourism with some U.S. export exposure; the province's renewable build-out ties to power prices and capital costs rather than to traded commodities.

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.analysis:
Yukon posted the highest participation rate of any jurisdiction at 75.0% in the June Labour Force Survey, with unemployment at 6.3% — the high participation1 accompanies a 2024 territorial GDP recorded at -3.3% on the annual provincial accounts, a multi-year-lag figure disclosed rather than extrapolated. CPI, housing starts, building permits, and wage growth are not published for the territory and are reported as N/A.

The Casino Mine, a proposed open-pit copper-gold-silver project, remains under Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Board review — project materials2 cite a $1.3B/year contribution to Yukon's economy over a 27-year life and roughly 132,280 FTE-years. The database tracks 113 Yukon projects, of which 105 qualify above the $3M threshold and total roughly $46.4B3; placer miners harvested $449M in gold revenue in 2025 with a record more than 2,500 gold claims issued.

Federal Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment ($40.0B, Proposed) is by far the largest tracked Yukon file, dwarfing the territory's resource projects — infrastructure (56 files), tourism_culture (16) and government (9) lead by count3, while gold and copper prices drive the resource files: Casino Mine ($3.6B), Kudz Ze Kayah ($489M) and Coffee Gold Mine ($317M).
provinces.sectorHighlights: Federal defence and resource mining anchor Yukon's tracked pipeline — the database records 56 infrastructure, 16 tourism_culture and 9 government files3. The $40.0B federal Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment dominates value, while gold and copper prices drive the resource files — Casino Mine ($3.6B), Kudz Ze Kayah ($489M) and the $363M Yukon Resource Gateway Project — and a record 2,500-plus placer gold claims tie territorial activity to the gold price2.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Yukon recorded the highest participation rate of any jurisdiction at 75.0%, a 70.3% employment rate, and a 6.3% unemployment rate in the June LFS — wage growth, CPI, and housing-starts sub-series are not published for the territory and are reported as N/A1. The 75.0% participation rate leads all jurisdictions, reflecting the territory's resource and public-sector labour base.
provinces.consumerPulse: Yukon's consumer-price and housing series are not published at the territorial level and are reported as N/A this period — the labour data1 shows a 75.0% participation rate and 6.3% unemployment, while placer miners harvested $449M in gold revenue in 2025, tying household activity to the gold price2. Resource-sector earnings rather than published CPI shape the territorial consumer picture.
provinces.marketContext: Yukon's pipeline spans 113 tracked projects, with 105 qualifying above the $3M threshold totalling ~$46.4B and only 4 tracked-unpriced; infrastructure (56), tourism_culture (16) and government (9) lead by count. The $40.0B federal Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment dominates value, while gold and copper prices drive the resource files.
provinces.tradeExposure: Yukon's economy is anchored in gold and copper mining with global commodity exposure; the Casino Mine and a record 2,500-plus placer gold claims tie territorial output to gold and copper prices.

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.analysis:
Northwest Territories posted unemployment of 7.9% and a participation rate of 71.5% in the June Labour Force Survey, against a 2024 territorial GDP recorded at -1.1% on the annual provincial accounts — the GDP figure1 is a multi-year-lag value disclosed rather than extrapolated; CPI, housing starts, building permits, and wage growth are not published for the territory and are reported as N/A.

Rio Tinto's Diavik diamond mine recorded its last official production day on 2026-03-24 after roughly 23 years and about 150 million rough carats — NWT real GDP is projected to decline to $4.0B in 2026, a 3.2% drop, as the diamond sector (about 25% of GDP at peak) winds down2. The territory is pivoting to critical minerals, with a study mapping 1,721 showings across 19 critical minerals, and the database tracks 88 qualifying NWT projects above the $3M threshold totalling roughly $46.8B3.

Federal Arctic defence dominates the tracked pipeline, led by the Arctic Defence and Infrastructure Spending Package ($35.0B, Proposed) and the Far North Early Warning Arctic Radar System ($2.5B, Proposed) — infrastructure (69 files), mining (56) and power_energy (19) lead by count3, while the Taltson Hydroelectricity Expansion Phase 1 ($1.2B, Under Construction) is positioned as foundational to diversification.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Federal Arctic defence and post-Diavik critical minerals anchor Northwest Territories' tracked pipeline — the database records 69 infrastructure, 56 mining and 19 power_energy files3. The $35.0B federal Arctic defence package and $2.5B early-warning radar dominate value, while the post-Diavik pivot ties the 56 mining files to critical-minerals and base-metals prices; the $1.2B Taltson hydro expansion adds power-sector capital exposure2.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Northwest Territories carried a 7.9% unemployment rate, a 71.5% participation rate, and a 65.9% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth, CPI, and housing-starts sub-series are not published for the territory and are reported as N/A1. The labour data accompanies the Diavik closure, which drives a projected 3.2% territorial GDP decline in 2026.
provinces.consumerPulse: Northwest Territories' consumer-price and housing series are not published at the territorial level and are reported as N/A this period — the labour data1 shows a 71.5% participation rate and 7.9% unemployment, while the Diavik diamond-mine closure on 2026-03-24 reshapes the territorial earnings base2. Critical-minerals diversification rather than published CPI frames the consumer picture.
provinces.marketContext: Northwest Territories' pipeline spans 205 tracked projects, with 88 qualifying above the $3M threshold totalling ~$46.8B; infrastructure (69), mining (56) and power_energy (19) lead by count. The $35.0B federal Arctic defence package and $2.5B early-warning radar dominate value, while the post-Diavik pivot ties mining files to critical-minerals prices.
provinces.tradeExposure: Northwest Territories' economy is pivoting from diamonds (Diavik closed 2026-03-24) to critical minerals with global export potential; the 56 tracked mining files tie territorial output to critical-minerals and base-metals prices.

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut posted the highest unemployment rate of any jurisdiction at 12.5% in the June Labour Force Survey, with a 65.0% participation rate, against a 2024 territorial GDP recorded at +7.5% on the annual provincial accounts — the GDP figure1 is a multi-year-lag value disclosed rather than extrapolated; CPI, housing starts, building permits, and wage growth are not published for the territory and are reported as N/A.

The Grays Bay Road and Port project advanced, with the federal government announcing up to $50M on 2026-05-20 through the First and Last Mile Fund for planning and preconstruction of an airstrip and wharf — an impact assessment2 projects the project could raise Nunavut GDP by roughly 20%. The database tracks 52 Nunavut projects, of which 41 qualify above the $3M threshold and total roughly $2.0B, the smallest territorial qualifying value3.

Nunavut now has three large gold mines projected to produce more than 1.2 million ounces in 2026, following the first gold pour at B2Gold's Goose Mine — Back River Gold Project ($610M, Under Construction) is the territory's largest tracked file3, mining/quarrying/oil-and-gas extraction was roughly one-third of NU GDP in 2024, and Baffinland's Mary River iron-ore mine (about 1,200 employees) is the largest private-sector employer.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Gold mining anchors Nunavut's expanding resource base alongside federal infrastructure — the database records 16 infrastructure, 6 tourism_culture and 6 mining files3. Gold prices drive the territory's mining base — Back River Gold Project ($610M, Under Construction) and a projected more than 1.2 million ounces across three mines in 2026 — while the proposed Grays Bay Road and Port (federal $50M preconstruction) would connect mineral-rich areas to a deepwater Arctic port2.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Nunavut carried the highest unemployment rate of any jurisdiction at 12.5%, a 65.0% participation rate, and a 56.9% employment rate in the June LFS — wage growth, CPI, and housing-starts sub-series are not published for the territory and are reported as N/A1. The 12.5% jobless rate is the highest of any jurisdiction this period, accompanying an expanding gold sector.
provinces.consumerPulse: Nunavut's consumer-price and housing series are not published at the territorial level and are reported as N/A this period — the labour data1 shows the highest jurisdiction unemployment at 12.5% alongside a 65.0% participation rate, while three gold mines are projected to produce more than 1.2 million ounces in 20262. Resource-sector activity rather than published CPI frames the territorial consumer picture.
provinces.marketContext: Nunavut's pipeline spans 52 tracked projects, with 41 qualifying above the $3M threshold totalling ~$2.0B, the smallest territorial qualifying value; infrastructure (16), tourism_culture (6) and mining (6) lead by count. Gold prices drive the territory's expanding mining base, while the proposed Grays Bay Road and Port would connect mineral-rich areas to a deepwater Arctic port.
provinces.tradeExposure: Nunavut's economy is anchored in gold and iron-ore mining with global commodity exposure; the territory's three gold mines and Baffinland's Mary River iron-ore mine tie output to gold and iron-ore prices, with the proposed Grays Bay port targeting export logistics.
